*Na vidyuḥ* means "they are not able to know"; the optative (*liṅ*) is used here according to the rule *śaki liṅ ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.172). He states the justification for this here with the word *pravāha*.
They are likewise said to be eternal like a stream; just as there is a continuous flow during every rainy season, so too there is an eternity of existence in every kalpa.

The meaning is: how could the greatness that is to be elaborated upon in the Sāmaveda fall within the scope of the intellect of those like us? Alternatively, the word "sahasra" signifies the immeasurable; [the greatness] is that which is to be propounded by an infinite mass of Vedas.
This is the meaning. //15//
"Having emanated," and so forth:
"of the *ṛc*s called *aghamaṛṣaṇī*s"— that is, those which dispel sin—
"emanation-free" (*nirmāyam*), meaning devoid of illusion (*māyā*).
*Kārmaṇa* refers to acts of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇakarman*); it is a metaphorical expression for a specific type of speech.
Halāyudha states: "Subjugation (*saṃvanana*) is *kārmaṇa*, which is the act of bringing [others] under one's control. (66)

The meaning is that the *Ṛgveda* is subject to your control. Alternatively, "kārmaṇa" refers to that ritual action which is performed for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśīkāra*) using the roots of medicinal herbs.
According to Amara, "the mūlakarma is the kārmaṇa" (67); having fashioned—that is, having performed—that [kārmaṇa], meaning having brought [it] under control.
Or else, *kārmaṇa* is simply *karman* itself, according to the rule "the suffix *aṇ* is added to *karman* when joined with that [word]" (68).

"In its own sense"; "endowed with that" means endowed with the meaning expressed [by the words]. The *Kāśikā* states: "That action which is performed exactly as one has heard it spoken is called *kārmaṇa*. (69) Having performed the ritual action conducive to the oral recitation of the *ṛc*s;
the meaning is: having carried out the purpose expressed by them. The reading is *unmārjati*; "not... [the rest of the sentence follows].
By the words "lokā" and so forth, the genitive case is prohibited. In the reading "unmārjanīḥ," the genitive would be characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix.
The meaning is: "by means of *ṛg* verses that destroy the sins of the world.
He whose "long-standing affection" (*praṇaya*)—that is, familiarity—is [present]; according to Amara, "affection" (*praṇaya*) may refer to familiarity or to a request. (72)
The meaning is that there is a long-standing curiosity in the mind upon hearing those words. "Mamārthavādaḥ" means praise concerning me—that is, praise having me as its object. //16//
The joining of palms is salutation, and that is for the purpose of conciliation; because it takes the form of conciliation, this is the limb called "attending upon" (paryupāsana).
As it has been said: "Worship and conciliation" (73).
*Aparyuṣitā* means "not stale"; the sense is: "May the boon be accomplished this very moment.
[The passage beginning with] "They remember," and so forth.

Regarding the majesty of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*): we are capable of knowing only this much—that at the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), they were the initiators of the Vedic tradition for the sake of benefiting the world. But as for the extraordinary power (*anubhāvaviśeṣa*) produced by specific ascetic practices (*tapoviśeṣa*), however...

"Vyatividrate" means they know one another; the construction is "then these very [people]. The augment *ruṭ* is applied by the rule "vetteḥ vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 7.1.6), and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by the rule "kartari karmavyatihāre" (Pāṇini 1.3.14). //17//
Regarding "samasyā" and so forth:
*samasyā* means a summary statement (*saṅgrahavākya*). Amarasimha states: "But *samasyā* has the sense of a compound (*samāsārtha*)" (76). The word "vā" [indicates an alternative].

The meaning is "like" (iva); that is, like a contracted form of the Sāmaveda. The suffix *kyap* is applied here by the rule "saṃjñāyāṃ samajaniṣada... etc., due to its frequent application (*bāhulakāt*). *Saṃvādaḥ* means a concordant statement (*sadṛśo vādaḥ*), one that establishes validity (*prāmāṇyasamarthakaḥ*).

*Paripaṇaḥ* means capital (*mūladhana*). Amara states: "The *nīvī*, *paripaṇa*, and *mūladhana* [are synonyms]. The *yajūṃṣi* (Yajurvedic formulas), however, signify profit; the intended meaning is that the play of your speech itself constitutes the *yajūṃṣi*.
The sense is that they are non-contradictory, like the Vedas. [The phrase] beginning with "relating to many objects" (*bahuviṣaya*) and so forth...
Its validity has been experienced many times; it is as if it speaks to one regarding what stands before them, because it is non-contradictory—this is the sense. Thus it has been said:

In the Bhāgavata Purāṇa: "For those who are free from envy, falsehood, hypocrisy, jealousy, violence, and pride, and who are of truthful character, their prayers are never rendered fruitless. (79) //18//
The sage’s smile was intentional, because Rāma alone was intended as the recipient of the boon;
with this very point in mind, it was said: "Where indeed do the words of the twice-born ever fail? (80)
Thus:
"davīyasya" and so forth. *Davīyasyaḥ* means "further away"; [this form is derived] by [the rule] *sthūladūra-* (Pāṇini 6.4.156).
Success! Even from afar, like objects situated at an extreme distance, they are difficult to attain. "Apatham" means a non-path, or a wrong way.
The meaning is that for one who possesses the blessings of the twice-born, there is no suffering even in the two worlds. [This refers to] the sentences;
"belonging to" (sambandhinaḥ); "not broken for very long" means belonging to a proximate time.

Thus they are unhandled; for that very reason, they are *khilāḥ*, meaning "uncultivated" (*aprahatāḥ*). Amara states: "The two words *khila* and *aprahata* are synonyms. When something has been scattered for a very long time, mere usage [of the items] is no longer possible. This is because they have not been scattered for an excessively long period.
In this regard, the meaning is that even the benedictions of Brahmins, which are rare in worldly discourse, occur only for certain meritorious persons and not for everyone.
Or alternatively:

Not long since broken [into pieces], they have had their transmission interrupted due to the absence of practitioners; for this very reason, they are "waste lands" (*khila*), meaning they have not been cultivated by students. As it is said: "The two [types of waste lands]—the uncultivated and the uncultivated by students—are equal. (83)
Thus says Amara.
*Kimapi* means possessing an indescribable power. *Malam* means suffering;
the meaning is that they sever the threefold afflictions, beginning with those internal to the self (*ādhyātmika*). Of *mṛjā*, which is purity...
The *majjānaḥ* (marrows) are the essential core (*sārabhūtāḥ*); according to Amarasimha, "the essence and the marrow are synonymous" (*sāro majjā samau*).
Where indeed do they change? By way of an interrogative intonation (*kākusvareṇa*), [it means] they do not change; that is to say, they are non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādinyaḥ*). //19//
"By means of indirect expressions (*vakrokti*), such as 'Where indeed do they go?

(85), which indicate the certainty that Rāma is his son-in-law; he 'bewilders'—the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here according to Pāṇini 1.3.74, *ṇicaśca*, and [the rule] 1.3.88, *aṇāvakarmakāt*."

Although this [objection] has been refuted by the prohibition "not with the foot" (88), it remains in that very state because of that prohibition. Of him—namely Viśvāmitra—for the sake of encouragement—that is, for the sake of gladdening. *Aviṣaṃvidānaḥ* means not knowing; the suffix *śānac* is applied according to the rule "samo gami" (89).
*Tīrtha* means a path.
Of the matter—that is, of the effect—consisting of the production [of the result] and the encouragement [to act].
The mention of the family first in the phrase "the two princes of Kakutstha’s lineage" is because, in marriage, the family is the primary consideration. This which is the "tīrtha"...
The construction is "it has been done.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of a son," and so forth: *jāṅghika* means swift;
*yayuḥ* refers to the horse intended for the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

"Yayus is the horse for the Aśvamedha sacrifice," according to Amarasimha. By this [epithet], "one whose fame wanders in that form," his status as a sovereign of the whole earth (*sārvabhauma*) is indicated; and by the word "king" (*rājñā*), his eligibility for the Aśvamedha is shown.

It has been stated; thus it is said: "The sovereign king (sārvabhauma) shall sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha). In that [sacrifice], there are four principal officiating priests (hotṛs)—namely, the Brahman, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ—who are present wherever [the rite is performed] in the horse-sacrifice.

He has bestowed the entire circle of the earth (*dattasarvabhūcakraḥ*). That the wealth arising from the circle of the earth itself constitutes a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) was demonstrated in the verse beginning with "kaccit kāntārabhājām" (92). As for *svaḥ*: those who dwell in heaven (*svarge*) are the "heaven-dwellers" (*svarvāsinaḥ*), namely, the gods.
In that regard, "sarvātithiḥ" means one who satisfies all; in that sacrifice (*makha*),
[it refers to] those human beings on earth, from the Brahmins down to the Cāṇḍālas.

"Those for whom all are guests are known as *sarvātithayaḥ*," according to Yādava. (93) "By himself" means by his own self (*ātmanā*); "yielding fruit" means [yielding] fruit by his own portion (*aṃśena*). This is because the word *sva* denotes that which belongs to oneself (*ātmīya*).

The intended meaning is that there is no other fruit similar to that action; thus, two instances of the instrumental case are used according to the rule: "An addition [to the rule] regarding the instrumental case is made from 'prakṛti' and so forth" (Pāṇini 2.3.18, vārttika 94). //20//
Regarding "tatkim" and so forth: *tat* refers to the result (*phala*). The question "Why these two alone? is asked.
By the word *kila*, which implies tradition (*aitihya*), a state of indirectness (*pārokṣya*) consisting of a traditional recollection is indicated; for this very reason, [the text says...]
The form *upāsāmbabhūvatuḥ* is the use of the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*). *Chidrāpidhānam* means the warding off of obstacles.
*Dakṣiṇā* refers to the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*).
By this, the excellent qualities of the bridegroom—noble birth, learning, character, heroism, and beauty—are described.
Janaka’s affection and high esteem are prompted by [his] capability and noble birth.
As for the word *katara*, it is formed with the suffix *ḍatarac* according to the rule *kiṃyattadaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.92).
Regarding the phrase "the four who... and so forth:
*Mālā-paramparā* means a succession of garlands. *Amlānā* means "not withered," because flower clusters (stabakas) do become withered over time; by this, its unimpeded nature is indicated.
*Jajñire* means they were born. *Acaramaḥ* means the eldest (*jyeṣṭhaḥ*). *Kālarātryāḥ* means of the Night of Destruction (*saṃhāra-rātryāḥ*).
*Pratyūṣaḥ* is equivalent to *prabhāta* (dawn), because it possesses the quality of destroying [darkness].
The mention of the crushing of Tāṭakā, who possessed the strength of a thousand elephants, is for the purpose of indicating his capability in breaking the bow. //21//

Regarding what was stated in the passage "The Slaying of Tāṭakā" (96)—that the sage’s assistance to Rāma was merely figurative—he says: "Excellent, O Blessed One," and so forth; [and] "among those such as we."
"Playing" here means looking toward others.
"With anger," and so forth: the "impact" (*sampāta*) of shame is its connection; by that, he is "blazing";
the meaning is that he is enraged due to his own defeat. "Agitated" (*sambhrāntaḥ*) means possessed of agitation.
The dance of old age belongs to the gods, because they are free from decay. //22//
[Tam apītyādi: Regarding the term *gopāyitāraḥ*, because it ends in the suffix *tṛn*, the sixth case (genitive) is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyaya-tṛnām*.
"Occurs," and so forth. "In the Guru" means in the presence of the Guru, by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
"The inner light" (*pratyagjyotiḥ*) refers to the inner self (*antarātman*).
It is like the satisfaction experienced upon beholding Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
The bliss born from the realization of Brahman has been relaxed; the meaning is that such [bliss] was not attained through Viśvāmitra’s arrival nor by service to the guru. //23//
"Sītā"—this is not [a name] for one who has descended; the sense is that they are recognized as being worthy of the status of husband and wife.
"This," and so forth: *praroha* means a sprout; [the state of] childhood.
The sense is: "Such is his prowess even now; how much more so in his youth!
The phrase "as if having accomplished his purpose" means as if he had obtained a bridegroom who would fulfill his vow.
Existence. //24//
The sage’s smile was intentional, implying that Rāmabhadra alone is the bridegroom.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the heart" (*hṛdayam*), the sense is that the desired fruit will be accomplished through the joy of the heart; as it has been said: "For in matters that are subjects of doubt for the virtuous..."
"The activities of the internal organ are the authority" (99).
Janaka’s distress is that he is unable to fulfill his promise;
he expresses this very point in the verse beginning with "yadgotrasya," etc. *Pravacana* means instruction.
*Śulka* is simply the bride-price; *setu* is an obstruction.
Here, by means of these three qualifiers, the qualities of the groom consisting of noble family lineage and greatness of character are expressed.

From here until the end of the verse, "Rulers of the earth enjoy [their lands] in vain" (100), is the *aṅga* named *vidhūta*, which consists of dissatisfaction caused by the inability to fulfill the tax obligation; as it has been said: "*vidhūtaṃ*... [and so forth].
"There may be dissatisfaction" (101). //25//
*Śulka* means a formal agreement or promise.
*Vimṛśan* means reflecting or deliberating; the ellipsis is that he is reflecting on the meaning of the phrase "this is nothing" (102).
"Yat" and so forth. *Argha* means price. He says this: "This is nothing at all," he says.
*Muhyati* means he is in doubt. //26//

He expresses the very doubt with the words "tadeva" and so forth: "Such [a thing]—having become weak through the power of the sage—might be merely attributed by the ignorant. "Jarjharaḥ" means "loose" or "flaccid. The sense is: "Or does the sage cause him to abandon his vow?"
This, being a statement characterized by indecision, is the ornament known as doubt (saṃśaya); as it has been said: "That statement which ends in indecision..."
"That is defined as doubt.

He says that neither of these exists, beginning with "difficult to overcome" (*durlaṅgham*) and so forth. "Difficult to overcome" (*durlaṅgham*) means difficult to mount. "Grasp" (*grahaḥ*) means insistence. The innate nature of his majesty (*anubhāvasya sahajatvam*) is due to Rāma being the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratvāt*). "Profound" (*gambhīram*) means immeasurable.
"Terrifying" (*bhīṣaṇam*) means unassailable. It is "extremely clear" (*atisphuṭam*) because of the slaying of Tāṭakā and others. //28//

"O Kauśika," [saying this] while conceptualizing—that is, while reflecting upon—your words, such as "if there were a system of tolls" (105), etc., [he asks]: "How can they be false? and so forth. "False conceptualizations" means unreal mental constructions.

"Having strung the bow and recovered Sītā, I shall sport with her in this manner"—such are the [thoughts]. How can I be satisfied by them? The word "already" (pūrvam) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Their unreality [is established] because the stringing of the bow was not even possible previously.
Previously, I was satisfied with the mere hope of Sītā’s marriage as if it were a sweetmeat; but today,
since the sage has requested the bow for the sake of my beloved, I shall become one whose resolve is true.
"Aha-ha" expresses distress.
Regarding "by the fool" and so forth: this action is the stringing of the bow.
*Pratyayita* means trustworthy; as it is said, "trustworthy (*pratyayita*) and reliable (*āpta*) are synonyms. (106)
Thus says Amara:
"Let the bow be brought," he speaks; in this manner, he deliberates.
He speaks secretly;
certainly. In this matter—regarding this point—what answer will he give? //29//
The king’s sigh was long and hot due to his certainty that stringing the bow was impossible. *Pratipādya* means having given;
[synonyms include] *viśrāṇanam*, *vitaraṇam*, and *sparśanam*.
"Pratipādanam" means "giving" (Amara-kośa 107).
Rāma’s shame arose from hearing the word "pratipādana" regarding Maithilī.

Regarding the passage beginning with *yatkodaṇḍa* and so forth: the absence of a bowstring (*jyābandharāhitya*) is due to the fact that the vow of protecting the world, which resides in himself, is not fixed upon the royal bows because it has been transferred [to them]. For this very reason, *rohitam* means straight; "the rainbow (*indrāyudha*) is the bow of Śakra, and that very thing is straight."
"Rohita" (108)—thus says Amara. "They too"—the meaning is that they are capable of protecting the world, which is Indra's duty. Of the calluses...

*Śyāmikā* is indeed blackness, which is *kastūrī* (musk); by that, they were made fragrant, meaning they were rendered weighty with excellence. As it is said: "Fragrance is the weightiness of virtue. (109)
Keśava,
having merely looked— not indeed taking [it]— [the others] feared to touch it upon seeing it.
Existence. //30//
By the words "Do you despise [me]? he refers back to the statement, "Where is such good fortune as that? (110).

"Tvadityādi" and so forth. "Tādṛśam" means that which accomplishes fulfillment by the surrendering of Sītā to Rāma. "Etādṛśām" refers to those [events] consisting of the marriages of Sītā and the others; by this, [the inclusion of] Lakṣmaṇa and the others is also indicated.
It indicates marriages. In the realm of fearlessness, they are "dānaśauṇḍāḥ," meaning generous givers; for "dānaśauṇḍa" means one who gives much (as stated in Amarakośa 1.11).
Thus says Amara;
the meaning is that these, however, are not like Rāmabhadra.

This is the ornament named *viśeṣaṇa* (qualification), which takes the form of a specific description (*viśeṣokti*) regarding well-known objects; as it has been said: "Qualification [consists in] [describing] objects that are already well-known..."
The proof of distinction. (112) Thus [ends the section]. //31//
"How so? and so forth. This [verse] is intended to exalt Rāma. "Desirous of speaking" means because he cannot endure the defeat of Rāma; this is the underlying sense.
*Ḍimbhāḥ* means children; [as it is said: "A *pota*, a *pāka*, and an *arbha*..."
"Ḍimbhaḥ" (113), according to Amara;
from here until "daśānanaḥ api" (114).

Because it consists in the pacification of the dissatisfaction caused by the inability to string the bow, it is called the limb named *śama* (tranquility); as it has been said: "The tranquility resulting from that is *śama*" (115).
Let Rāma be such [as described].
He states that the bow is likewise extraordinary with the words beginning "by Girīśa" and so forth.
*Ārāddham* means worshipped; *avajaitram* means victorious. //32//
*Prapañcikā* means expansion. This is the power of Rāma; we hold it in high esteem—that is to say, we trust in it. Regarding the phrase "producing," etc.: *kuṇapa* means a corpse.

"They devour" means *kauṇapāḥ*, i.e., *rākṣasāḥ* (demons). The suffix *aṇ* is used here as a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*). According to Amara, "a corpse (*kuṇapa*) is neuter. In the reading *koṇapa*, *koṇa* means blood.
"Those who drink" are the *koṇapās*; [the word] *koṇa* is used for a specific type of musical instrument,
and *koṇa* is not feminine when it means a club or the son of the Sun (Mars).
"Also in the method of playing the lute and other instruments, and in a corner of the house," according to the *Viśva* lexicon.
[He was] performing a fire-oblation with ten million of those [offerings], intending to produce [the result].

The *laṭ* (present tense) is used for the future when there is proximity to the present time. By this, the destruction of Rāvaṇa and others is indicated as occurring very soon. *Tejaḥ* is indeed majesty; it is fire. *Sāmidhenīm* refers to the placing of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) for the purpose of kindling [the fire].
The word "verse" (ṛc) is prescribed; by it, the *samidh* wood is indicated: "A verse that serves as a *sāmidhenī* or a *dhāyyā* is used for the kindling of the fire. (120)
Thus says Amara. The sense is that Rāma’s splendor has increased ever since the slaying of Tāṭakā.
"By childhood friends" means by those used for childhood play.
The meaning is: "by means of fruits fashioned from wood and so forth.

*Īṣajjayaḥ* means "conquerable with little effort"; the suffix *khal* is used in the sense of ease (*akṛcchra*). Here, the third case ending is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) according to the rule *anena*; [this is prohibited] by the rule *na loka*.
By these and other such statements, the genitive case is prohibited. The mention of Rāvaṇa is for the purpose of indicating the arrival of Śauṣkala. //33//
The partial entry onto the stage is due to fear of the king and the necessity of making a representation.
The name Śauṣkala is derived from the cause of eating meat; for it is said: "One who eats meat (āmiṣāśin) is a Śauṣkala" (124).
Thus says Amara. Regarding the form *didṛkṣate*: by the rule *jñāśrusmṛdṛśāṃ sanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.57), the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) suffix is applied.
The word *ā* is used in the sense of anger; Amarasimha states: "The word *ā* may be used in the senses of anger and affliction" (126).
This is also used to express disagreement.
The permission for entry [is granted] due to the connection with Rāvaṇa.
From here until the end of the section on "the great festival" (127),
this is the dramatic element named *nirodha* (obstruction), because it consists of the obstruction [of Rāma and the others] for their own benefit.
As it has been said: "The obstruction of what is beneficial is *nirodhana*.
Regarding the phrase "the service of the bow," he designates the very act of stringing it as "service" (*paricaryā*), and by the term "great festival" (*mahotsava*), he refers to its source.
"Marriage. Regarding the phrase "when half-spoken":
the remaining half is "and the great festival of Sītā’s wedding."
Thus,
this is the dramatic element known as *narma*, consisting of words intended for jesting; for this very reason, there is the expression "he laughs."
As it has been said: "Jesting speech is *narma* (jest).

The section ending with "she looks at him out of the corner of her eye" is the dramatic element named *narmadyuti* (the brilliance of jest), because it consists in the manifestation of composure regarding the subject of the jest.

As it has been said: "Fortitude is considered to give rise to radiance" (130). And this fortitude is to be inferred from the side-long glance, which is an ensuant (*anubhāva*) of anger caused by the imposition of an unintended meaning.
"Of all"—that is, of us all Rākṣasas—he is the enemy.

This is the intention of Śauṣkala; however, the truth is that Viśvāmitra means "the friend of the universe" (*viśvasya mitra*), with the lengthening of the vowel according to the rule *mittre carṣau* (Pāṇini 6.3.131).
This is the ornament known as the *Nirukta*.
As it has been said: "Etymological derivation (nirukti) is the connection [of a word] with its meaning by way of its constituent parts. (132)
"By the right hand" means in a place not far to the right of the hand, according to the rule beginning with *enabanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 5.3.35).

The suffix *enap*; [by the rule] "the second case ending is used with words ending in *enap*" (Pāṇini 2.3.31), as in *puṇya-enam* and so forth. From the word *lakṣmī*, the suffix *kap* is applied by the rule "after feminine stems ending in long *ī* or *ū*, and after those ending in *ṛ*" (Pāṇini 5.4.153). *Vīra-upakaraṇa* = the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*).

That in which the subordinate element appears is thus: the *śānta* (tranquil) rasa is present in Rāma because of his *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) nature; it functions as an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). The *śānta* rasa is an accessory (*upakaraṇa*) to the *vīra* (heroic) rasa in Lakṣmaṇa because of his *dhīroddhata* (noble and haughty) nature.

And because it is endowed with knowledge (*vidyā*), and because its gender is fixed, it does not have a neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅgatva*). [The term] "mauñjyādayaḥ" means that of which the "vyañjanas"—that is, the manifestors (*vyañjaka*)—beginning with the girdle of muñja grass (*mauñjī*) and so forth, are the primary ones; by the word "ādi" (etcetera),...

The excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*) of the sentiment of tranquility (*śānta-rasa*) are the ascetic practices (*brahmacarya*), such as the staff and the black antelope skin; these serve as both the objective supports (*ālambana*) and the ornaments (*alaṃkāra*).
The excitants of the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*) likewise consist of the objective supports and their ornaments.
Furthermore, the bow, arrows, and so forth, which are characteristic of the kṣatriya status, are also mentioned. //34//
"Pārśva," and so forth: the three possess a similarity to the Triple Veda (*trayī*) because of their peacefulness (*śāntatva*).
They are characterized by two forms—that is, by their own essential natures (*svarūpa*).
Because the ritual portion (*vidhibhāga*), which consists solely of instruction, is tranquil, it is equal to Rāma;
whereas the mantra portion (*mantrabhāga*) consists of [terms such as] *khaṣ*, *phaṭ*, and *jahi*.
Thus, by virtue of his ferocity arising from a direct connection with the act of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) of such a nature, he possesses a resemblance to Lakṣmaṇa. //35//

"Hātaka" is a term of reproach. "Anuplavamānaḥ" means following or imitating. "Īdṛśāt" refers to one of little strength; for this very reason, he is called a "child" (*ḍimbha*). "Tādṛśaḥ" means of the nature of death.
"Daivasya" means of fate or destiny; "durvipākaḥ" means a wicked result. "Te" refers to her who possesses the strength of a thousand elephants—this is the intended meaning. [Thus spoke] Anaraṇya.
There was a king named Aikṣvāka who was killed by Rāvaṇa; he lacked self-knowledge,
for even upon hearing of his own son Anaraṇya’s condition, he himself acted treacherously toward Rāvaṇa.
This is the state of being.
He explains that very point with the words beginning "Sunda," etc. "Sunda's son" refers to Subāhu;
the meaning is that his prowess was formidable due to the slaying of him.

The "family" (kuṭumbaka) refers to the group of dependents, such as Tāṭakā and others. That she herself acts hostilely toward Rāvaṇa for the sake of the sage’s acquisition of fruit demonstrates her lack of self-knowledge (anātmajñatva). //36//

*Śauṇḍīrya* means pride (*garva*); it is derived with the suffix *ṣyañ* according to the rule for words beginning with *brāhmaṇa*. It should be understood that the intention is "I shall destroy [it]. The word *miśra* is a term used for those who are venerable due to their learning and seniority; by that—
The absence of boldness (*śauṇḍīrya*) is indicated.
From this point until the end of the passage, "to the house of you, the protected one" (138),
it is classified as *puṣpa* because it consists of specific statements in the form of clever speech (*caturukti*).
The name is a constituent element; as it has been said: "A sentence possessing a specific [name] is like a flower.
By the term "descendant of Pulastya," he indicates a lack of heroism due to being the son of a Brahmin.
He rebuts [the opponent] by suggesting that even something unwholesome might be considered wholesome through a question about virtue— namely, "those of the king. By this,
he expresses his own dependence on Rāvaṇa.

Regarding the passage beginning with "āpadām" and so forth: by the word "atharvabhiḥ," the absence of both intelligence and courage is indicated; for this very reason, [the king] is to be protected by a domestic priest (purohita).
"Those like you" means those endowed with mantras; the sense of "ill-behaved" also flashes forth [in the mind].

This statement is made because the duty of the domestic priest (*purohita*) consists in the remediation of calamities; regarding this, the *Nītivākyāmṛta* states: "One should appoint a domestic priest as the remediator of calamities, both divine and human. (140)
*Anuyujyate* means "is questioned"; as Amarasimha states: *praśno 'nuyogaḥ pṛcchā ca* (1.6.20).
What is being questioned? Prosperity and adversity [are determined] by one's voice.
indicated. //37//

By the word "śrotriya," he expresses a lack of heroism. In the sense of "we would have countered" (*pratyakariṣyāma*) and "it would have been" (*abhaviṣyat*), the conditional (*lṛṅ*) is used for the future in cases of the non-occurrence of an action (*kriyātipatti*). A *mattavāraṇī* is a railing at the edge of a platform intended to prevent one from falling.
The dwarf-like wall is made of wood; the chest itself is the palace because it is the abode of Śrī; its stability is like that of a *mattavāraṇī* (the elephant-stall);
and because he has conquered all the worlds, the sense is that no calamity can come from anywhere.
He says that very thing in the passage beginning with "yac ceṣṭā" and so forth. *Samanīkam* means battle.
*Parāñcan* means fleeing.
Desiring to conquer Pātāla, he uprooted Kailāsa as if for the sake of a path to go there.

"Upādāna" means the cause. The sense is: for one who has conquered heaven and the netherworld (pātāla) and lifted up Mount Kailāsa, what indeed could be called a calamity from humans, who are as insignificant as blades of grass? //38//
Arjuna with a thousand arms refers to Kārtavīrya.
"Avalīḍha" means devoured.
"For great [beings]... and so forth; "such as these" means exactly like Rāvaṇa.

"Great ones"—the meaning is, how much more so Rāvaṇa? Therefore, the implication is that defaming a great person brings about fault. Not only is there greatness [in him], but his audacity as well is truly extraordinary; this he states with the words beginning "Furthermore," and so on.
"Syātām," and so forth. *Hehaya* is the name of a particular region; its lord was Kārtavīrya.
"Avagāḍha," and so forth: this means that their mental strength had entered [the enemy], that is to say, they had come to know Rāvaṇa’s true essence. *Pratiṣṭhā* refers to majesty.

He says that very thing in the verse beginning with "sadyaḥ" and so forth. *Kīkasam* means bone; as Amarasimha states: "Both *kīkasam* and *kulyam* mean bone. *Pallavena* means by the hem [of his garment]. *Prāsphoṭayat* means he caused it to burst open clearly.

The meaning is "he wiped me. The word "by himself" (svena) expresses his affection; for this very reason, there is the excellence of Skanda. Victory and defeat depend upon destiny, yet Rāvaṇa possesses peerless majesty due to the grace of Hara.
Existence. //39//
"Maghonaḥ," and so forth. *Alasīkṛtya* means having rendered [him] incapable of action.

*Svārājyam* means the sovereignty of heaven; he *bhunakti*, i.e., protects it; because the root has the sense of protecting, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is not used (cf. Pāṇini 1.3.66). *Avacchidya* means having taken away by force.

The sense is that while his arms alone are fickle, his fortune (śrī) is indeed steady. He causes Fortune to dwell—that is, to reside—in the forest of his arms. The charm of fickleness lies in its being the cause of moving about at will; this is because it is common [to all].
The concentration on the state of being restrained. //40//
"Contented," and so forth. Contentment [arises] even from the cutting off of one's head.
*Kaṇḍūlam* means "itching."

[The suffix] *la* occurs after [the root] *sidh* and others (Pāṇini 3.2.145). "Desiring to obtain" (*lipsuḥ*) means desiring to acquire. "From dejection" (*dainyāt*), "turned away" (*parāñci*) means turned away from it;
the meaning is that they could not endure his dejection.

*Mithaḥ* means mutually (*parasparam*). *Kalahāyante* means they engage in quarreling (*kalahaṃ kurvanti*); the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied here according to the rule beginning with *śabdavaira* (Pāṇini 3.1.17). //41//
"So too" (so'pi): the particle "api" is used here in the sense of possibility.
"A maiden," and so forth; "born without a womb" (ayonijanmānam);
[this refers to those] such as those born from the moisture of the womb (*garbhakleda*) and the like.

The sense is that there are no faults; and the further sense is that because she is not one's own biological daughter (*anaurasatvāt*), one should not harbor prideful attachment toward her. *Varītum* means "to request" (as in *vṛta*).
The vowel *vā* (147) is long. Regarding the phrase "of the protected" (*guptasya*) and so forth:
it is a praise of the domestic priest (*purohita*), meaning "you are beyond the reach of force."

"Even he who, out of a desire for his own purpose, harbors pride even toward the Lord, now begs of you"—this is Janaka’s encouragement. By saying "me," it is also implied: "Since you are not protected by valor, you did not come yourself; rather, being 'protected by your priest,' you have sent me, who am endowed with ascetic power. //42//
The passage beginning with "pinākadarśana" (the sight of the Pināka bow) is contrary to the speech of Śauṣkala, as well as the awakening of Janaka.
Regarding the phrase "kimiti" and so forth: "etadeva" refers to the Pināka [bow] for Rāma.

"It should be shown" means "once again. He connects this with the sentence beginning with "Show that bow," and so forth. The word "abhidhīya" (being addressed) is used in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*).

*Laṭ*: the third person singular ending. "Dependent on you" (*tvayā paravantaḥ*) means "subordinate to you" (*tvatparādhīnāḥ*), the sense being that we shall act exactly as you have instructed; for "dependent on another" (*paratantraḥ*) is synonymous with "subordinate to another" (*parādhīnaḥ*).
"Paravān means 'one who has a protector' (nāthavān)," according to Amara-kośa. //43//
The mention of "space" (ākāśa) means that it is not an answer, because it was spoken by one who is not an authoritative witness; the meaning is that it is "not an answer.
"Difficult to determine" means impossible to decide. "Even an answer" [is likewise].
"Let there be no gift of Sītā; rather, give me something else."
This is a sarcastic remark (*solluṇṭhoktiḥ*). From here until the end of the passage ending with "Maithilī will be fashioned" (151),
there is the dramatic element named *pragama*, because it consists of a series of successive statements.
As it has been said: "Just as the subsequent speech is the progression" (152).
He himself instructs the way to provide the answer: "This [speech] must be given," and so forth. *Masṛṇam* means smooth, that is, not harsh;
the sense is that no one else is capable.
To us—meaning for us—your deeds, which transcend the realm of passion (*parorajāṃsi*), meaning they are characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*), proclaim [this truth];
that is, they declare: "One must proceed toward the work of the virtuous" (*satkārya*). This is the intended meaning. //44//

"Śāmbhava," and so forth. "Pūrṇapātra" (the full vessel) refers to an object forcibly seized by friends during festivals; as it is said: "That which is seized by friends during festivals by force, such as clothing, ornaments, and the like, is called *pūrṇapātra*."
"That has been stated by the wise," says Yādava (in his lexicon). The meaning is: "This Sītā is not to be given away; rather, she is to be won by oneself once the bow has been strung. //45//
"Of you too"—the word "too" (*api*) is used here in the sense of reproach; it means "of those who are weak.
"These syllables"—this refers to the statement: "I shall not give them to you, for you are incapable."
The sense is that this is improper.
From here until the end of the passage, "of your mother Ahalyā" (154),
this is the dramatic element named *vajra*, because it consists of harshness directed at the person present.
As it has been said: "The vajra is directly harsh.
Regarding the phrase "by that" and so forth, and "by a hundred fingers," this is because he possesses twenty arms;
as it has been said: "He has ten faces..."

"Having twenty arms and four legs, it is a temple of measurement. (156) Thus, "rubbed by him" means uprooted; by this, the absence of effort is indicated. By the expression "the mountain of Kubera," the connection with one who is not a lord [of the world] is stated.
He states the absence of hostility toward Śiva:
"whose prowess is explicitly stated"—that is, mentioned directly in each word—belonging to the very sprouts that are his arms;
whose prowess [is known] precisely by the lifting of Kailāsa.
The meaning is that it became clear. "By the Māheśvara [bow]" is the reason for its not being strung. "This is such-and-such" means "it is like this";
it is like the word *tattādṛśa*. "Un-Aryan" means contemptible; it does not mean difficult.
[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. Could it be produced?
The meaning is that it is certainly not produced by means of sound (*svara*). //46//
"This," and so forth. "Of Kṣatriya lineage" is the reason for establishing the proposition (*pratijñā*).
Because [the word] *āropayitṛ* ends in the suffix *tṛn*, [the genitive case is not used] by the rule "not in connection with *loka*" (*na loka-*) and so on.
In connection with a verbal noun (*kṛt*), the genitive case is prohibited. Regarding the word "jānāsi" (you know):
the meaning is that non-giving itself constitutes the answer. //47//
"O devotee of Maheśvara," and so forth. "Insignificant" means those incapable of retaliating against Rāvaṇa, or alternatively, those incapable of lifting [the bow]. What will you become?
Or what calamity will you encounter? You will perish even before being consecrated by marriage, or even once married to him.
The meaning is that you will surely be taken captive by Rāvaṇa himself. //48//

The *adhikāra*—meaning the subject matter or introduction—is present here; thus, by the suffix *ṭhan* in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), it refers to a particular treatise. In this [treatise], everyone [should abandon] pride in their strength regarding the bow.

"Having avoided [this], he becomes disciplined"—this is what is meant. He applies this to the present context with the words "As for today," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "Rāvaṇa too": by the word "too" (api), his wickedness is indicated.
He states that very point with the words "Of Śambhu," and so forth. By the term "support" (ādhāra), there is a suggestion of his treachery toward his master.

"Aho" is used here in jest; the sense is: what kind of insolence could there possibly be on the part of one who is fearless even in uprooting the very foundation [of the world] when it comes to stringing that bow? //49//
*Avahitthā* is the concealment of one's outward appearance.
(160) Regarding the passage beginning with "tadetad" and so forth: *pratiruṣitā* means pervaded. It is an empirical fact that wherever there is heat, there arises turbidity. By you...
The intention is that when the bow is drawn, those who consider themselves heroes should become pale; and this was said with reference to Rāvaṇa. //50//
"Are you? is a word of contempt. "Udbhrānta" means insane.

"Adhikṣepa" refers to [boasting of] the heat of one's valor and so forth. Regarding "in our presence": the sense is that disparaging one's own master in the presence of servants is rooted in arrogance. Gairika...

The classification of elements (*dhātubheda*). "Pota" means a young one or an infant. How is this lack of discernment yours? The meaning is: from where has it come? "Duli" means a female tortoise; according to Amarasimha, "the female tortoise is *duli*" (1.8.162). By the word *duli*...
Drops pervading that body are perceived;
the meaning is that the eyes are equal to that [body].
"From the mother":
the meaning is that this grasping of non-existent objects has come to you through a succession of causal excellences.
"Before us" means: "I shall not take you into account.
"Dry" means fruitless; the sense is that a quarrel with this person, who is incapable of obstructing our purpose, is useless. "A guest" means: he is worthy of honor.
The sense is that he is not worthy of opposition.
The distress of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa arises from the obstruction of their welfare, namely the stringing of the bow.
Regarding the phrase "with humility" and so forth: humility [is defined] by the presence of a teacher.
Because of the effort toward marriage out of shame and curiosity;
[the suffix] *apādāna* is used for a marvelous action.
"Excellent," and so forth. *Karmādbhutam* means a wonder in the form of an action.
*Vailakṣyam* [is used] because of the inability to repay the favor. "By which," meaning by the head. "That," meaning the embarrassment.
"Even the three worlds"—by the word *api* (even),...

He states that [the goal] is not to be requested because it is to be accomplished by one's own arm alone. Regarding the word *arthī*: in the sense of "one for whom wealth (*artha* = *dhana*) is not present," the suffix *ini* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.118 (*arthāccāsannihite*); thus, it means "one who possesses desire."

The masculine gender is used because it represents the state of being a beggar; the *Nyāsa* states: "And here, by the very nature of its denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*), it refers specifically to one who possesses desire. For primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*) are characterized by their denotative function. //51//
Regarding the passage beginning with *yasmin*: *khaṭvāṅga* is the bone of the spinal column.
*Ākṛṣṭaḥ*; the words "up to the ear" (*karṇaparyantam*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis. *Pureva* means "as before";
this is stated because it serves as a residual ornament for Śiva. Of that [bow], which has become a bowstring...
The word "api" (also/even) is used because of the contradiction between being an earring and being a bracelet.
By mentioning the breaking of the bow of Bhārgava— the guru who was the slayer of Kārtavīrya when attacked by Rāvaṇa— it is shown that Rāvaṇa was weaker than Rāma.
It was indicated;
the mention of "the preceptor of Bhārgava" (Paraśurāma) is intended to suggest the arrival of Bhārgava, who had come enraged by the breaking of his preceptor’s bow. //52//
"Obstructing," and so forth: *rundhan* means deafening; *kroḍayan* means gathering together into a mass.
Regarding the eightfold nature of the principal mountain ranges (*kulaparvata*), there are seven principal mountains for each of the eight regions (*varṣa*).
This is with reference to the group of eight principal mountain ranges (*kulācala*).

As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "O great sage, those regions such as Kimpuruṣa and the rest, which are eight in number... beginning thus, and continuing: "...in all these regions there are seven [mountains]."

"There are seven mountain ranges" (166); and in the *Brahmasiddhānta* as well, beginning with: "In the eight-petaled lotus of the earth, with the feet [of the directions] as its filaments and Sumeru as its pericarp, the Supreme Lord is worshipped by those who know Him."
"Every year, a hundred rivers and seven-seven [forty-nine] principal mountain ranges [are destroyed]," (167). Thus, those who are deaf to their own eyes—
Because he is "one who has ears like a snake" (*cakṣuḥśravas*), the third case ending is used according to the rule *yenāṅgavikāraḥ*.
The eight families of Nāgas are named Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Śaṅkha, Karkoṭaka, Pauṇḍraka, Patra, Kelāputraka, and Jambhaka. By this [is meant] Kolāhala’s...
The pervasion of the three worlds is indicated. By the word "dalati" (it splits), he expresses Rāma's lack of effort regarding its destruction. //53//

Janaka’s joy arises from obtaining the boon, his despondency from the breaking of Śiva’s bow which he had set aside, and his wonder from Rāma’s prowess; thus, the phrase "how could it be broken? expresses these three states of mind.
The word *api* is used here [to indicate inclusion].
Regarding "Vaidehī" and so forth: *kandaraḥ* means a cave; as Amarasimha states, "A cave (*darī*) is called *kandaraḥ*" (1.2.3). *Ulūluḥ* refers to auspicious occasions such as weddings.

The specific singing of women [is the object]. Regarding the word "dviṣatām" (of the enemies), the genitive case is used for the object according to the rule beginning with "jāsiniprahaṇa" (Pāṇini 2.3.56).

*Upaśruti* is an accidental statement that determines the intended meaning. *Dambholi*-ness [is attributed] because of its impenetrability and its unbearable sound. The metaphorical representation of the roar as being composed of *sūkta*s and so forth occurs in relation to the mouths of the twice-born and others.
Because of its resonance. //54//
Śauṣkala’s despondency arises from the failure of his undertaking, while its marvelous nature results from his extraordinary prowess.
"Sarvakarmīṇam" means pervaded by all activities such as battle; the suffix *kha* is applied according to the rule "tat sarvādeḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.7).

*Ūṣmāyitam* means the emergence of heat (*ūṣmodgama*). [The form is derived] by adding the suffix *kyaṅ* according to the rule *bāṣpoṣmabhyām udvamane* (Pāṇini 3.1.16), and then the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) suffix in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*); it thus means "strength. By the word *sphuliṅga*, he intends "childhood. For in the world...
The heat of a spark is not capable of performing actions such as cooking, whereas this [heat] is; hence the exclamation "Aho! (how wonderful!).
"This one," and so forth.

She was "bought" by means of the "quality of the self"—that is, by the price consisting of the joy of the self through having strung the bow; the sense is that she was not given by me [as a gift]. This was for the sake of "transaction," which consists of the roles of giver and receiver.
The dative case in "lakṣmaṇāya" indicates a gift.
From this point until the end of the passage, "Everything must be arranged by us" (174), is the dramatic element (aṅga) called *upanyāsa*, which consists of a conciliatory proposal.
As it has been said: "The introduction [of a topic] is clarification" (175). //55//
Viśvāmitra’s smile was due to the attainment of his intended marriage with Lakṣmaṇa;
Karṇa said, "It is just so."

The meaning is: having said, "Request Bharata and Śatrughna through Māṇḍavī and Śrutakīrti. *Pāritoṣika* means that which arises from satisfaction (*paritoṣa*); [this is derived] by the rule *tatra bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53).
*Ṭhak*: You bear or carry [it]; "also mine" is in the genitive case because there is no status as a creditor (*uttamarṇatva*).
"What do you intend? means "What do you desire?"; the word "tell that" is to be supplied. (177)

In the context of a conciliatory request for taking the hand [in marriage], the phrase "wait" (*āgamayasva*) and so forth implies a delay; the meaning of the word *tāvat* is that once Daśaratha has arrived, we ourselves shall give [the bride] later. For this very reason, the term "wait" (*āgamayasva*) is derived from the root *ā-gam*.

"The ātmanepada [suffix] should be prescribed for the root *kṣam*. Thus, the ātmanepada is used. According to the *Kāśikā*, "forgiveness (*kṣamā*) means indifference (*upekṣā*), i.e., the passing of time.
A "messenger of entrusted purpose" (*niḥsṛṣṭārtha*) is an envoy who possesses independent authority regarding both peace and war.
Thus it was said by Kauṭilya: "He whose actions regarding peace and war with the master are authoritative is one who has full discretionary power (*niḥsṛṣṭārtha*), such as Kṛṣṇa."

"Of the Pāṇḍavas" (180), and so forth, beginning with "the play of the arms. Here, because the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas are included by the phrase "and among the descendants of Ikṣvāku," there is the constituent element (*aṅga*) called "the synthesis of the social orders" (*varṇopasaṃhāra*).
As it has been said: "The merging of the four castes is intended as the dissolution of the castes" (181).
Here, the term *cāturvarṇya* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for multiple castes. //56//
"Smayamānaḥ" means laughing. "Puruṣa," etc.:
"Bahirangāṇi" means secondary or non-essential;
you, though an elder, are like a child because of the absence of association with the learned.
The meaning is "thus. *Prahīṇam* means ownerless wealth. *Yaunasambandhāya* means for the sake of marriage.
*Upasthitam* means arrived or obtained. *Varṣīyān* means old; [according to Pāṇini 6.4.157] *priyasthira-*... (182)
By such statements, the passing of the year and so forth is indicated. "Tender" (*komalā*) means incapable of worldly activity.
"Not yet," and so forth; "does not transgress" (*nātikrāmati*) means does not pass beyond [the time], because even now there is an absence of the sacrament of marriage.
The sense is that it is possible to cause [the girl] to be given to Rāvaṇa, who is the most excellent groom;
as it has been said: "One may take back even a daughter already given if the groom is more excellent."
"Let him come" (183)—this refers to Rāvaṇa as a "false archer"; the sense is that he is not a superior suitor.
"Kadarthita" means tormented.

*Ātmānam* means the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇam*). *Pacelimaḥ* means cooked (*pakvaḥ*); [the suffix] *kelimar* is added according to the rule "the addition of *kelimar* is prescribed" (Pāṇini 3.2.4, vārttika 184). *Agadaṅkāraḥ* means a physician (*vaidyaḥ*); [the suffix] *kāra* is added according to the rule "after *satya* and *agada*, [the suffix *kāra* is added]" (Pāṇini 3.2.5, vārttika 185).
"O ascetic woman, you are to be pitied; you are ruined, meaning that your ultimate welfare is lost.
He says the same thing in the verse beginning with "tribhuvana... and so forth: "You are not independent."

Since you have arisen from the earth, even your mother and others do not exist [as prior causes]; therefore, who produces—that is, brings about—your status as the object of Rāvaṇa’s love, even more so than the Goddess of Victory (Lakṣmī) who conquers the three worlds? By way of sound (svara), the meaning is: no one at all. //57//
"By means of ancient [verses]," and so forth. *Gāthāḥ* = *ślokāḥ* (stanzas).

*Arthāpitāḥ* = rendered purposeful; the meaning is that they were taken up as subjects to be described through a spirit of competitive excellence (*ahamahamikayā*). This is used in the sense of "one who performs that" (*tat karoti*).

The causative suffix *ṇic* is established by the rule "artha-veda" (Pāṇini 3.2.187). The metaphorical representation of the pillar (*stambha*) is due to its similarity to deceit (*māyā*) in terms of its deceptive nature and firmness (*dārḍhya*).

The transformation into the nature of the thunderbolt (*dambhola*) is for the purpose of serving the function of drying up the pride that has arisen; and thus, these are the two ornaments known as *rūpaka* (metaphor) and *pariṇāma* (transformation).

There is no room for the suspicion of a tautology of ornaments resulting from the presence of two forms; as it has been said: "Metaphor (rūpaka) is simply simile (upamā) with its distinction obscured" (188). Furthermore: "That which is superimposed, existing as the very nature of the object of superimposition, when it serves the purpose of the subject at hand, is [the figure] pariṇāma."

Thus it has been stated. (189) And: *utprekṣya* means having remembered. *Mada* itself is *maireya*, which is *āsava* (distilled liquor); according to Amarasimha, "maireya, āsava, and śīdhu [are synonyms for liquor]. (190)

In the phrase "in the rows" (*śreṇīṣu*), the locative case indicates the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Previously, because Airāvaṇa’s tusks were always fresh, they were constantly enjoyed by the celestial bees; however, at another time, they became stale.

There was a distinction between the ornaments and the garlands; however, today, due to the recollection of Rāvaṇa’s arms and their resulting loss of pride, they have become like withered garlands—this is the meaning. "Withered" (*yātayāma*) implies a state of similarity [to the ornaments]. Or rather: previously...
Formerly, it was enjoyed by bees because of its intoxicating state; but now, even though its intoxication has departed,
it has become worthy of being served by bees due to its constant nectar and its adornment with celestial garlands.
This is the meaning. Regarding the state of being frequented by bees, there is commonality. //58//
"In them" means "in those arms. The intention is that even later on, he will lead [the enemy] away by the strength of his arms alone.

"Vṛthā," and so forth. By means of the relationship—that is, by the cause consisting of being the father-in-law of Rāvaṇa—there was the honor performed by the world; by that [honor], he was "deceived," meaning abandoned.
Alternatively, "vṛthāsajjanāḥ" means that Daśaratha and others were not true *sajjana*s (virtuous men).
The meaning is that they come into being; therefore, the implication is that there is no connection with them even as a cause for honor.

The intended meaning is that it is not, however, something to be enjoyed. [The form] "bhaviṣyate" is used; here the periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) is employed in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). (191)//59//
"Samantāt" and so forth: "uttālaiḥ" means lofty;
"taraṅgaiḥ" means by successions [of waves]. His very arms are "parighas," a specific type of weapon, because they are the cause of victory. Of that [arm]...
"Saurabhya" means the weightiness of virtues (guṇagaurava); "pratāpa" and "parimala" are synonyms. The mention of "wind" is used because it brings forth fragrance. "Cetasi kṛtām" means remembered.

Regarding the phrase "ruler of the three worlds": because she is desired by the king, she is not to be taken as a wife; therefore, do not take her—do not marry her. The implication is: for one by whom even celestial women have been made captive, how insignificant is the taking of a human woman? //60//
"Profound" means immeasurable. "Having placed the task before him" means that his reliance on the company of ministers is for the purpose of deliberating upon the prevention of future calamities.

It is called an *aṅka* (act) because it contains the direct experience (*pratyakṣa*) of Rāma’s deeds; for instance, following the interruption caused by the quarrel with Śauṣkala and others, there is the subsequent matter of Bhārgava’s victory, [introduced by the words] "O teacher of Bhārgava... and so forth.
Because of the proximity of the sentence "The bow is drawn," which takes the form of a *bindu*, [the following applies].
And because it is the locus for the flavor of various kinds of dramatic arrangements.
Thus ends the third act in the *Anargharāghava-pañcikā* composed by Viṣṇu, son of Muktinātha.
